title: Choosing a Git Workflow
description: Evaluate your team context and choose the right Git workflow: Git Flow, GitHub Flow, GitLab Flow, or trunk-based.

data.text: There is no universally best Git workflow. The right choice depends on your team size, release frequency, deployment model, and organizational maturity. This lesson provides a decision framework for selecting the workflow that fits your context.

data.title: Key questions to ask
items: **How often do you deploy to production?** Continuous → GitHub Flow or TBD. Scheduled → Git Flow.
**Do you need a stabilization period?** Yes → Git Flow with release branches. No → simpler models.
**How large is your team?** Small (<10) → GitHub Flow or TBD. Larger → Git Flow or GitLab Flow.
**Do you have feature flags?** Yes → TBD or GitHub Flow. No → Git Flow may be safer.
**Is your CI/CD mature?** Yes → simpler models. No → Git Flow provides more safety.
**Startup shipping daily**: GitHub Flow or TBD with feature flags
**Enterprise with quarterly releases**: Git Flow with develop and release branches
**Regulated industry (finance, healthcare)**: GitLab Flow with approval gates and environment branches
**Open-source project**: GitHub Flow with maintainers merging PRs

data.title: Start simple, evolve as needed
data.text: Do not adopt Git Flow on day one of a new project. Start with GitHub Flow or trunk-based and add structure only when pain points emerge. Premature process is worse than no process.

Regardless of which workflow you choose, track DORA metrics (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, MTTR). These metrics tell you whether your branching strategy is helping or hurting your delivery.

items.question: Can I switch workflows mid-project?
items.answer: Yes, but it requires coordination. Communicate the change, update your CI/CD pipelines, and give the team time to adjust.

items.question: Does workflow choice affect Git commands?
items.answer: Yes. Git Flow users use git flow commands. Others use standard Git with conventions. The underlying Git mechanics are the same.

items.question: What if my team uses a hybrid model?
items.answer: Hybrid models are common. Many teams use Git Flow for release management but require daily integration to develop or main. Document the hybrid explicitly.

items.question: Should I let developers choose their own workflow?
items.answer: No. A team needs a shared workflow for coordination. Choose one, document it, and enforce it with CI rules.

data.text: The Same Change in Three Workflows

The workflows differ in the branch topology, not in the Git commands. Seeing the same feature shipped through each one makes the trade-off concrete: the number of long-lived branches, where integration happens, and how a release is cut.

data.title: GitHub Flow: short branch, PR, merge to main, deploy
data.code:
# Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull --ff-only

# One short-lived branch per change
git switch -c feature/AUTH-123-login

git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint"
git push -u origin feature/AUTH-123-login

# Open a PR, get review, merge to main (squash or merge)
# main is always deployable, so merging triggers the deploy
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feature/AUTH-123-login

data.title: Git Flow: feature branches integrate into develop, release is cut from it
data.code:
# Features branch from and merge back into develop
git switch develop
git switch -c feature/AUTH-123-login
git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint"
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feature/AUTH-123-login

# Cut a release branch when you freeze for stabilization
git switch -c release/1.4.0 develop
# only bug fixes land here
git commit -m "fix(auth): correct token expiry"
git switch main
git merge --no-ff release/1.4.0
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"

# Back-merge the hotfix into develop so it is not lost
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff release/1.4.0

data.title: Trunk-based: short-lived branches and feature flags
data.code:
# Branches live hours, not days; integrate at least daily
git switch main
git pull --rebase
git switch -c auth-123-login

git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint"
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push -u origin auth-123-login

# Merge behind a flag so incomplete work never blocks the release
git switch main
git merge --ff-only auth-123-login
git push

# The flag controls exposure; the code is already on main

data.title: Interview angle: workflow choice is a team decision, not a Git feature
data.text: The commands are identical across all three workflows; what changes is how often you integrate and how many branches live at once. Trunk-based development needs strong CI and feature flags because unreviewed work reaches main quickly; Git Flow needs discipline to back-merge fixes so develop does not drift. When asked which to choose, answer from release frequency, CI maturity, and team size, then name the cost of the one you picked — that is the answer interviewers are listening for.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Choose a workflow based on release frequency, team size, and CI/CD maturity
Start simple — adopt complexity only when pain points demand it
Git Flow suits scheduled releases; GitHub/TBD suit continuous deployment
Track DORA metrics to validate that your workflow is helping
Document the chosen workflow and enforce it with branch protection rules
